newsitem.title: UK: S&P cuts Veritas Reinsurance claims paying rating.
newsitem.headline: S&P cuts Veritas Reinsurance claims paying rating.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Thursday it lowered its claims-paying ability rating on Veritas Reinsurance Co. Ltd. to BBB minus from BBB.

It said the move followed Wednesday's conclusion of the agreement of its German parent, VHV Vereinigte Haftpflicht Versicherung V.a.G (VHV) to sell Veritas to U.S. investors with financial and reinsurance expertise.

In addition, Standard & Poor's said it assigned its BB minus rating to the $135 million senior notes due 2003 of Veritas Holdings GmbH, a German limited liability company that was arranged to effect the acquisition of Veritas from VHV.

"The downgrade primarily reflects the discontinuation of the parental relationship with VHV and the resulting uncertainty over Veritas' emerging business position in the long term," S&P said in a statement.
The agency said the issuance of a seven-year debt to pay for the acquisition will impose considerable financial leverage on the new company structure.

S&P said Veritas' relationship with VHV will change in the long term, from ownership to negotiation and arms-length business arrangements, which may not provide the same level of profitability as in the past.
However, Veritas reinsures a stable book of business, 48 percent of which is a German private motor quota share treaty with its parent, it said.

"This treaty will remain in effect for the next nine years, thus providing a stable base for expansion of the non-VHV business," S&P said. "Moreover, VHV has guaranteed incurred but not reported reserves up to 89.6 million Swiss francs.
Veritas is dependent on the German market, particularly the motor insurance market, since about 75 percent of its net premium is derived from German insurers on a proportional basis.
European deregulation has put pressure on price, a trend already apparent in Germany, S&P said.
The company's purchase will also be partially debt- financed, which will boost debt to capital ratio to 63 percent in 1997, falling to 41.5 percent in 2002.
The existence of substantial debt and the termination of the parental relationship with VHV will decrease the company's financial flexibility.

S&P also noted the company's good capital position. It said although capital has not been a strength historically, Standard & Poor's projects Veritas to have more than sufficient capital to support its total premium growth over the next 10 years.
S&P said it expects that earnings from VHV and non-VHV business will be sufficient to retire the debt and still maintain capital at a high level.
